canonical_definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats logical reasoning as a latent model ability to derive valid conclusions from premises, rules, facts, or constraints by applying formal logic, often through multi-step deduction. Many definitions stay close to this premise-to-conclusion framing, including deduction from rulebases, first-order logic formulas, or natural-language premises, and some papers make the operation explicit with examples such as inferring an equivalent statement like "B is A" from "A is B". A smaller line of work broadens the construct to include inductive or abductive inference, critical thinking and robustness, contradiction detection and internal consistency, or recognition of abstract token patterns, so the main disagreement is between a narrow formal-deductive ability and a broader family of reasoning or coherence abilities, and between latent capacity and observable task performance.

Space of facets. Papers most often systematize the construct into reasoning subtypes rather than a single undifferentiated skill. Several explicitly place deductive, inductive, abductive, and analogical reasoning under logical reasoning, while others carve out narrower forms such as syllogistic reasoning, propositional inference, first-order logic reasoning, disjunctive reasoning, formal inference, and multi-domain deductive reasoning. Related labels including logical deduction, deductive reasoning, logic inference, logical inference, and simply logic are used for closely overlapping capabilities, and some evaluation frameworks further package it with dimensions such as logical correctness, robustness, efficiency, or coherence.

Space of measurement. Operationalization is overwhelmingly benchmark-based: papers link logical reasoning to 42 measurement instruments and 12 behavioral indicators. The most frequently linked instruments are FOLIO, LogiQA, PrOntoQA, ProofWriter, and ReClor, alongside many other instruments; these are described as benchmarks for deductive questions, conclusion-from-premises tasks, ontology-derived logic problems, small rulebases of facts and rules, and standardized exam-style logical reasoning. Other linked instruments extend the construct into multimodal, long-context, agent, and broader reasoning evaluations, so measurement sometimes tracks the dominant formal-deduction definition closely and sometimes bundles it with wider reasoning or task performance. Among behavioral indicators, chain of thought is the most recurrent, alongside action selection, argument generation, code generation, and constrained text generation, and several papers operationalize the construct through intermediate reasoning steps, explanations plus conclusions, or consistency-checked rationales.

Links. Beyond measurement, papers link logical reasoning to 22 constructs. The most recurrent links say it is related to abductive reasoning, inductive reasoning, in-context learning, legal reasoning, and logical consistency, with many other constructs also appearing; several papers explicitly treat deductive, inductive, abductive, and analogical reasoning as types within the same family. Causal claims are more scattered and usually appear in single papers: some papers claim causal relationships from prompting or perception-related behaviors to logical reasoning, including from in-context demonstrations, chain-of-thought prompting, and fine-grained perception, while one paper reports a causal relationship from code generation to logical reasoning in which performance is degraded on Date Understanding. Other single papers claim causal relationships from logical reasoning to downstream outcomes such as consistency, safety-oriented performance, and task-level decision or prediction behaviors.

characterization_sections.label: Space of definitions.
characterization_sections.text: Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats logical reasoning as a latent model ability to derive valid conclusions from premises, rules, facts, or constraints by applying formal logic, often through multi-step deduction. Many definitions stay close to this premise-to-conclusion framing, including deduction from rulebases, first-order logic formulas, or natural-language premises, and some papers make the operation explicit with examples such as inferring an equivalent statement like "B is A" from "A is B". A smaller line of work broadens the construct to include inductive or abductive inference, critical thinking and robustness, contradiction detection and internal consistency, or recognition of abstract token patterns, so the main disagreement is between a narrow formal-deductive ability and a broader family of reasoning or coherence abilities, and between latent capacity and observable task performance.

characterization_sections.label: Space of facets.
characterization_sections.text: Papers most often systematize the construct into reasoning subtypes rather than a single undifferentiated skill. Several explicitly place deductive, inductive, abductive, and analogical reasoning under logical reasoning, while others carve out narrower forms such as syllogistic reasoning, propositional inference, first-order logic reasoning, disjunctive reasoning, formal inference, and multi-domain deductive reasoning. Related labels including logical deduction, deductive reasoning, logic inference, logical inference, and simply logic are used for closely overlapping capabilities, and some evaluation frameworks further package it with dimensions such as logical correctness, robustness, efficiency, or coherence.

characterization_sections.label: Space of measurement.
characterization_sections.text: Operationalization is overwhelmingly benchmark-based: papers link logical reasoning to 42 measurement instruments and 12 behavioral indicators. The most frequently linked instruments are FOLIO, LogiQA, PrOntoQA, ProofWriter, and ReClor, alongside many other instruments; these are described as benchmarks for deductive questions, conclusion-from-premises tasks, ontology-derived logic problems, small rulebases of facts and rules, and standardized exam-style logical reasoning. Other linked instruments extend the construct into multimodal, long-context, agent, and broader reasoning evaluations, so measurement sometimes tracks the dominant formal-deduction definition closely and sometimes bundles it with wider reasoning or task performance. Among behavioral indicators, chain of thought is the most recurrent, alongside action selection, argument generation, code generation, and constrained text generation, and several papers operationalize the construct through intermediate reasoning steps, explanations plus conclusions, or consistency-checked rationales.

characterization_sections.label: Links.
characterization_sections.text: Beyond measurement, papers link logical reasoning to 22 constructs. The most recurrent links say it is related to abductive reasoning, inductive reasoning, in-context learning, legal reasoning, and logical consistency, with many other constructs also appearing; several papers explicitly treat deductive, inductive, abductive, and analogical reasoning as types within the same family. Causal claims are more scattered and usually appear in single papers: some papers claim causal relationships from prompting or perception-related behaviors to logical reasoning, including from in-context demonstrations, chain-of-thought prompting, and fine-grained perception, while one paper reports a causal relationship from code generation to logical reasoning in which performance is degraded on Date Understanding. Other single papers claim causal relationships from logical reasoning to downstream outcomes such as consistency, safety-oriented performance, and task-level decision or prediction behaviors.
